text: Given the root of a binary tree, return its nodes' values in preorder.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — preorder means: at every node I take the node first, then the whole left subtree, then the whole right subtree. Same rule at every node. Is that right?

Then let me name the property that matters most here, because I want to use it later. Preorder output always has the shape root, then the whole left subtree, then the whole right subtree — three blocks, back to back, never mixed. So two facts fall out. The first value is always the root. And the answer splits into three runs that sit next to each other.
Can the tree be empty? And are there any constraints on the input size?
It can be empty — return an empty list. Up to one hundred nodes, any shape, int values.

Let me run through the example. Root one has children two and three. Two has children four and five, five has children six and seven. Three has only a right child, eight, and eight has a left child, nine. Preorder: root one, then the whole left side, two, four, five, six, seven, then the whole right side, three, eight, nine. You can see the three blocks right there in the answer.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to read the tree level by level with a queue and then reorder the values into preorder. That doesn't work cleanly — a level mixes values from different subtrees, so I'd have to rebuild parent links to unmix them. More work and more risk, for the same linear time. This problem reminds me of a plain depth-first search. Preorder is literally the order DFS first touches each node. The definition is recursive, so I'll write the recursion and let the call stack do the bookkeeping.

Here's the plan. One: if the node is empty, return. Two: push the node's value. Three: recurse left, then right. I'm using one shared vector passed by reference, and every call only appends, so the three blocks land in order by themselves. One thing worth flagging — inorder, preorder and postorder are the same function; only the position of the one push back line changes. So I'll pick my test tree carefully: on a right-leaning chain, preorder and inorder give the same answer. The smallest tree that separates all three is one, two, three. There's a trade-off here: preorder is easy to write iteratively with a stack, but with a hundred nodes the recursion is safe and reads like the definition, so I'll go recursive. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function makes an empty vector, calls the helper on the root, and returns it. The helper is exactly the plan: stop on null, push the value, recurse left, recurse right. One thing worth flagging — the base case is root equals null, not a leaf check. A leaf check would crash on the empty tree and on any node with one child, and every leaf would return before its push, so leaf values go missing. With null as the floor, a leaf needs no special case. And the ampersand on the vector is required — without it each call fills its own copy, and a non-empty tree returns an empty list.

Let's dry-run the code on the same tree, expected one, two, four, five, six, seven, three, eight, nine. The row that matters is step one: the root is pushed before any recursion, so it can only be first. After it, the block column reads five left-subtree values, then three right-subtree values — three runs, back to back. That contiguity is exactly what makes rebuilding a tree from preorder plus inorder possible. That matches. Corner cases: an empty tree hits the base case and returns empty. A single node pushes one, then two empty calls. One, two, three gives three different traversals, so it catches a misplaced push back.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: exactly two n plus one calls, one per node plus one per empty link, because an n-node binary tree has exactly n plus one empty links. Each call is constant work, and push back is amortized constant. Space is O of h for the call stack, where h is the height; the output vector is linear, but that's the answer. In the worst case the tree is a chain, so h equals n; balanced, it's about log n. If the tree could be huge and skewed, I'd switch to the iterative stack version — push root, then pop, emit, push right, push left. Oh, one more thing — the tree is only read, never changed, so it's safe to traverse again or share between readers.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You named the output shape up front — root, then the whole left block, then the whole right block, never interleaved — and used it to explain why rebuilding a tree from preorder plus inorder works. You pointed out that all three traversals are one line's position apart. And you followed that through to test design: you rejected a chain because it can't tell preorder from inorder, and picked one, two, three as the smallest tree that separates all three. Good work.
